hints: Look at Fig. 4.2 for the link that joins one sugar ring to the next - focus on the oxygen bridge between the two rings, not the bonds inside a ring.
walkthrough:
Spot What Joins Monomers Together**
Think of chitin like cellulose, a long chain of sugar monomers. Inside each ring there are C-C and C-O bonds, but only one special bond connects ring 1 to ring 2. That is the glycosidic bond and it always contains an oxygen atom acting as a bridge.

Circle the Correct Bridge**
In Fig. 4.2 the central O linking the left ring to the right ring is the glycosidic bond. Circle that O and its two connecting lines. Do not circle the O inside the ring or the side groups like CH2OH, NH or OH.
Final answer: Circle the C-O-C oxygen bridge between the two N-acetylglucosamine rings (the 1-4 glycosidic bond).

hints: Remember what hydrolysis does - it is the reverse of condensation, so water is added across the bond you just circled to split the chain.
Think about where the -H and -OH from water go - each broken end of the glycosidic bond regains an -OH group, so check carbons C1 and C4.
walkthrough:
Reverse Condensation With Water**
A glycosidic bond is made by condensation, which removes water. Hydrolysis by chitinase adds water back: $C-O-C + H_2O \rightarrow C-OH + C-OH$. So the long chain is split into separate rings.

Add Back The Two OH Groups**
Draw one hexagonal monomer exactly as shown in Fig. 4.2, keeping CH2OH, NHCOCH3 and other OH groups the same. The key change is to put an -OH on C1 at the right side where it was joined to the next sugar, and ensure there is an -OH on C4 at the left side. Those two -OH groups show water has been added.
Final answer: Draw a single N-acetylglucosamine ring with -OH added at C1 (where it was linked to the next monomer) and -OH present at C4.

hints: Start by reading Fig. 4.3 carefully - compare the bar heights for not filtered versus filtered and state the size of the drop with units.
Link filter pore size to copepod size - the fabric traps anything larger than $20 \mu m$, so think about what is removed with the copepods.
Explain why filtering does not give zero cases - think about what is smaller than $20 \mu m$ and can still get through.
Think beyond the water itself - suggest another way people could still catch cholera or another difference between families that filter and those that do not.
walkthrough:
Describe The Trend**
Water not filtered shows about 1.2 cases per 1000 population, while water filtered through folded fabric shows about 0.6 cases per 1000. So filtering roughly halves cases, which supports that filtering helps prevent cholera.

Explain The Reduction**
V. cholerae lives attached to the surface of copepods. Copepods are animals about 1 mm long in Fig. 4.1, much larger than $20 \mu m$, so folded fabric traps them and removes most attached bacteria from drinking water.

Explain Why Cases Remain**
Not all bacteria are attached. Some V. cholerae live free in water and are far smaller than $20 \mu m$, so they pass through. Very small copepods may also pass through. That is why filtered water still causes about 0.6 cases per 1000 rather than zero.

Suggest Other Variables**
Cholera is faecal-oral, so infection can also come from contaminated food or other water sources. Families who take time to filter may also have better general hygiene, e.g. hand washing, or boil water, which could also lower their rate. Correlation alone does not prove filtration is the only cause.

Final answer: Filtering reduces cholera from approx. 1.2 to approx. 0.6 cases per 1000; filtering removes copepods > $20 \mu m$ carrying V. cholerae on surface; some free bacteria / small copepods pass through fabric so some cholera remains; transmission via other sources e.g. food or differences in hygiene / other water treatment.

hints: Cholera spreads by the faecal-oral route, so apart from cleaning water, focus on how faeces could reach the mouth via hands, food or flies.
walkthrough:
Block The Faecal-Oral Route**
V. cholerae leaves the body in faeces and must be swallowed to infect the next person. Purifying water is one block, but you can also block transfer on hands, food and flies.

Give One Qualified Behaviour**
A good answer needs detail, not just wash hands. For example: wash hands thoroughly with soap after defecation and before handling food, or wash fruit and vegetables in uncontaminated water, or keep food covered so flies cannot transfer bacteria from faeces to food.

Final answer: Wash hands thoroughly with soap after using toilet / before preparing food; or wash fruit / vegetables in clean water; or cover food to prevent flies; or avoid crops grown with untreated faeces as fertiliser.

hints: The clue is location in the cell surface membrane plus use of ATP - what type of membrane transport needs ATP and a carrier protein?
If the protein pumps something out of the cell, think about how that would change the concentration of tetracycline inside where it normally acts.
walkthrough:
Recognise Active Efflux**
A membrane protein that uses ATP is doing active transport against a concentration gradient. Here it is an efflux pump, meaning it moves a substance outwards.

Link Pumping To Resistance**
Tetracycline needs to stay inside the bacterium to stop protein synthesis. By actively pumping tetracycline out as fast as it enters, the internal concentration stays too low to kill the cell, so V. cholerae survives and is resistant.
Final answer: Protein acts as efflux pump for active transport; uses ATP to transport / pump tetracycline out of the bacterial cell so it cannot act.

hints: Compare targets - an antibiotic often attacks one site, while a vaccine can present several different antigens to the immune system.
Compare timing and population size - think about when a vaccine acts versus when an antibiotic is given, and how that affects the chance a resistant mutant is already present.
walkthrough:
More Mutations Needed To Escape Vaccines**
Antibodies from a vaccine often recognise several different antigens. A single mutation might change one target for an antibiotic, but to escape a vaccine the bacterium would need several mutations at once to change all antigens, which is much less probable.

Timing Favours Vaccines**
Vaccination is given before infection, so memory cells mount a fast secondary response and kill the small invading population before mutants can arise and divide. Antibiotics are given after a person is already ill, when billions of bacteria are present, so there is a far higher chance a resistant mutant already exists and is then selected. Misuse of antibiotics also increases selection pressure.

Final answer: Vaccines contain multiple antigens so multiple mutations needed for immune evasion; vaccines act before infection via rapid secondary response when pathogen numbers low; antibiotics used after infection when population large so resistant mutant more likely / antibiotics target single site / more likely misused.
